storySpine.want: Sing the opening of the Iliad through to the end without stopping or being prompted.
storySpine.obstacle: In the middle of a line her memory goes blank, in front of a waiting, laughing crowd.
storySpine.turn: Philon shows her that the song is built from set phrases, and those phrases are what carry a singer.
storySpine.outcome: She begins again, lets the phrases carry her, and reaches the end of the opening without stopping.

changed: Rewritten as an imagined scene for younger readers, centred on a young singer at a festival on Chios. The wording, the order and the invented apprentice are ours.
storyNote: The festival singing, the invocation to the Muse, the epithets, the oral telling and the two poems are from the record, as are Chios and Ionia. Myrto, Philon and their evening are invented.
story:
The Homeric poems were sung for a long time before they were written down. Singers performed them at religious festivals, in front of crowds. Many stories about the poet came later. The most common said he was a blind bard from Ionia. This scene is imagined. It is one evening on the island of Chios, in Ionia.

Chios was one of the places people named as the poet's home. Myrto, who was twelve, was learning the songs. There were two of them. The Iliad told of a quarrel between King Agamemnon and the warrior Achilles. That quarrel filled the last year of the Trojan War. The Odyssey told of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, and his ten-year journey home after the fall of Troy. Tonight Myrto had to sing the opening of the Iliad on her own.

The opening was an invocation to the Muse. The singer asked her to sing of the anger of Achilles. The crowd knew the words as well as Myrto did. She began.

Her voice was steady for a few lines. Then it was not. In the middle of a line she could not find the next word. She stopped. The crowd waited. Someone laughed.

The evening was warm, and the lamplight was low. Myrto wanted to run out of the courtyard. Then an old singer crouched beside her. His name was Philon.

He did not tell her to try harder. He asked for the next few words, and she gave them. Then he said two words: 'Rosy-fingered Dawn.'

He showed her that the song was built from set phrases. The singers called them epithets. There were many: 'rosy-fingered Dawn', 'owl-eyed Athena', 'crafty Odysseus'. A singer did not hold every word in his mind at once. The phrases carried him forward. The same phrases helped singers make the song again, in many places, for many years. That was how a long poem could live in a voice instead of a book.

Myrto began again. 'Sing,' she sang, 'of the anger of Achilles.' This time the next words came. The phrases were like stepping stones across a stream. The next phrase was there: rosy-fingered Dawn. She reached the end of the opening and did not stop.

Here the imagined scene ends. What the record holds is this. The songs were passed from singer to singer, and only later were they put into writing. They were not the work of one language alone. They were made in Homeric Greek, a literary language that mixed older dialects of different centuries. Today scholars still debate who made them, and whether one poet or several did.

claims.text: The Homeric poems were originally transmitted orally.

Homer frequently uses epithets such as "rosy-fingered Dawn", "owl-eyed Athena" and "crafty Odysseus".
These habits aid the extemporizing bard and are characteristic of oral poetry.
